newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zulu leader denies knowing of S.African hit squads.
newsitem.headline: Zulu leader denies knowing of S.African hit squads.

text.p: South Africa's Zulu leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi on Wednesday denied any knowledge of apartheid-era hit-squad killings in his home province of KwaZulu-Natal.

Daluxolo Luthuli, who led a group of men from Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) which was trained by the white regime in counter-revolutionary warfare, alleged on Tuesday that Buthelezi had full knowledge of the group's actions.

Luthuli and two other hit squad members have told the Truth and Reconciliation Commission that they were trained to kill political opponents of Inkatha because of attacks on IFP supporters by now President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) and its United Democratic Front allies.

"My client, Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi, said he is astounded by these allegations. He denies any knowledge of hit-squad activities," Patrick Falconer, Buthelezi's lawyer, told the Commission on Wednesday.
"Many high-profile people in this country are being implicated in these hearings. Once these cases are stated they cause irreparable damage."
Buthelezi was given advance legal notice that he and several of his party leaders would be implicated during the hearings.
He asked Pretoria's army in the mid-1980s to help him set up a force to protect himself and his party from attacks and threats from the ANC.
The apartheid-era government approved a plan at the highest level, which entailed covert military training in Namibia's Caprivi Strip.
Falconer said Luthuli's statements, made to reporters outside the truth commission on Tuesday, were a legal offence and demanded an apology.
But Luthuli's lawyer Angus Stewart said Luthuli stood by his statements.

"Mr Luthuli makes no apology for the statement he made. He reiterates and stands by his statement which was that Chief Buthelezi must have known about hit-squad activities that took place and that were carried out and conducted by the Caprivi trainees," Stewart said.
Luthuli also implicated Buthelezi's right-hand man, Zakhele Khumalo, as the one who ordered all the killings and who had supplied the squads with weapons.
Another hit-squad member Zweli Dlamini told the commission on Wednesday recruits were trained to kill political opponents.
"We were trained, and knew we were trained, to only kill. Our enemy was the United Democratic Front (UDF) which was operating in our areas. If we met UDF members we shot them," he said.
"When we entered houses we shot everyone there."
Some 15,000 people have been killed in over a decade of fighting in KwaZulu-Natal between Inkatha and the ANC.
The truth commission was set up by Mandela to try and get to the bottom of apartheid-era crimes committed by both sides and to foster reconciliation through confession and apology.
